claims.text: Conventional casting can produce a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine lamellar FCC/B2 dual-phase microstructure.
Rapid, short-duration high-temperature annealing after moderate cold rolling will partially heal lamellar interphase boundaries.
Rapid, short-duration high-temperature annealing after moderate cold rolling will slightly coarsen the lamellar interfaces.
The treatment will improve coherence between the ductile FCC and hard B2 phases.
The treated interfaces will promote activation of additional slip systems.
Brief annealing will relieve local internal stresses at the lamellar interfaces.
Brief annealing will restore dislocation mobility at the lamellar interfaces.
The annealing treatment will retain the deformation-refined microstructure rather than sacrificing it.
Relieving interfacial stresses and restoring dislocation mobility will mitigate stress concentrations.
Maintaining a fine-scale lamellar microstructure contributes to high strength.
Fine lamellar FCC/B2 eutectic HEAs can exhibit a balance of high fracture strength and high ductility.
Relative to an identically cold-rolled but unannealed baseline, the treated alloy will have higher yield strength.
Relative to an identically cold-rolled but unannealed baseline, the treated alloy will have greater tensile elongation.
The simultaneous strength and ductility improvement will occur under room-temperature tensile loading.
The beneficial effect is expected in eutectic HEAs having a balanced FCC/B2 phase distribution.
Excessive annealing temperature or duration will cause excessive microstructural coarsening.
Excessive coarsening will diminish both strength and ductility.

contradictions.description: The intervention field defines the intervention as cold rolling plus annealing, whereas the hypothesis, baseline, and controlled experiment treat cold rolling as common preprocessing and annealing alone as the tested intervention.
